# Public accounts, audit and budget (`public_accounts_audit`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by double_entry, arabic_numerals, representative_government
- Core idea: Everyone who handles public money must keep written accounts and present them at fixed dates to auditors who are independent of him, can demand receipts, and can charge him personally for what is missing. Next step: income and planned spending are set out in one yearly budget, approved in advance, and the accounts are published. Theft and waste are then visible, the ruler learns what he can afford, and lenders and taxpayers can see where the money goes. The separation of the one who orders a payment, the one who pays and the one who checks is the core rule.
- Pitfalls:
  - Auditors who depend on the people they audit find nothing
  - Auditing honesty but not purpose: accounts can balance while the money is wasted
  - Publishing flattering figures: Necker's Compte rendu (1781) showed a surplus by leaving out war spending and helped ruin French credit when the truth came out
  - Accusing a minister of theft at court without proof and protection is a quick way to be destroyed by him
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2100–2000 BC – Ur III state archives balance receipts and issues of grain, silver and labour per official, with yearly balanced accounts; greece: 5th–4th c. BC – every Athenian magistrate undergoes audit (euthyna) by boards of accountants on leaving office; public accounts cut in stone; india: c. 3rd c. BC–3rd c. AD – Arthashastra describes a records and audit office, yearly closing of accounts and fines for officials who under-report revenue; china: Qin and Han – yearly accounts sent up from every county (shangji) and checked by the chancellery; censors investigate officials; islamic: c. 780 – Abbasid diwan al-zimam, a bureau that controls the accounts of the other departments; americas: 15th c. – Inca khipu-keepers account for storehouse contents and labour dues, checked by inspectors; europe: c. 1110–1130 – English Exchequer audits sheriffs twice a year on a chequered counting cloth (oldest pipe roll 1130); c. 1320 French Chambre des comptes; 1689 Parliament votes supply yearly; 1861–1866 British Public Accounts Committee and Comptroller and Auditor General
- Read:
  - Jacob Soll, The Reckoning: Financial Accountability and the Rise and Fall of Nations (2014)
  - Richard FitzNigel, Dialogus de Scaccario (c. 1179)
